chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, all from Ibn Mahboub, from Ibn Raib, from Abu Ubayda, from Suwayr who said:

I heard Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) saying: 'The angels, when they hear a believer supplicating for his believing brother in his absence, or mentioning him with goodness, say: You are a good brother to your brother, for you supplicate for him with goodness while he is absent from you, and you mention him with goodness. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has given you double what you asked for him, and lauded upon you double what you lauded upon him, and for you is the merit over him.'

And when they hear him mentioning his brother with evil and supplicating against him, they say to him: You are an evil brother to your brother! Refrain, O you who is veiled over his sins and his private parts, and be still with yourself, and praise Allah who veiled over you, and know that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is more knowing of His servant than you are.

key_terms.الْمُسَتَّرُ عَلَى ذُنُوبِهِ: the one veiled over his sins
key_terms.بِظَهْرِ الْغَيْبِ: in his absence / behind his back

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual reward for supplicating for a brother in his absence?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi highlights the spiritual efficacy of du'a for the absent brother, emphasizing the principle of 'double reward' (mithlay ma sa'ala lahu) as a divine incentive for selfless intercession. Scholarly tradition interprets the angels' rebuke for evil as a reminder of Allah's superior knowledge (Allahu a'lam bi-'abdihi), encouraging believers to conceal faults rather than expose them, aligning with the virtue of satr (concealment of sins).
